Fishermen from the opposite shore crossed in summer to dry their catch on the flats, and a few families cut turf for fuel and abandoned their huts each winter. The first recorded grant of land dates from the 1620s, when a merchant from the coast was given rights to take timber from the eastern bank. The town's growth was checked by the wars with France, which cut off the Baltic trade and left many of the yards idle. A gasworks was constructed near the station, and a subscription library, a mechanics' institute and a savings bank all appeared within a decade. The municipal corporation was reformed in 1835, and the older guilds gradually lost their privileges. Drainage schemes in the 1860s removed the last of the marshes, and the reclaimed ground became the site of the cattle market and the new cattle sheds. The town's principal grammar school was founded in 1564 by a local wool merchant, and for three centuries it remained the only school in the district. Its endowments were administered by a body of trustees who also controlled the almshouses and the common land, and their minutes, which survive from the 1590s, are the fullest record of everyday life in the town before the nineteenth century. The school moved to larger premises on the edge of the town in 1872, and the old building served for a time as a corn exchange. By the end of the nineteenth century the town had a population of some nine thousand. Its industries were still dominated by shipping and by the processing of agricultural produce, though a small engineering works had begun to manufacture agricultural machinery for export. The twentieth century brought a gradual decline in the harbour trade, and the last commercial vessel left the quay in 1968. Much of the waterfront was redeveloped for housing in the 1980s, and the surviving warehouses are now listed buildings.
